item.description: a long three quarter jacket worn by men. Characterised by having three fastening buttons. Worn on special occasions or for Sunday use.
this word seemed to be preferred to ‘cotan’. Was used to mean cotton or calico.
home-made cloth used to make dresses and skirts – ‘còta drògaid’.
undyed wool used to make underwear. Flannel-like substance.
connected with the above [i.e. clòmh bàn (q.v.)], this means the criss cross pattern made when underwear was being sewn together.
soot was used as a dye for wool, as was heather and iris root.
rush-like plants found on machair land and whose roots were used to obtain dye.
rheumatism.
rupture, hernia.
appendicitis.
bladder related illness.
swelling of the throat affecting horses.
sore throat, tonsillitis.
mumps.
seal oil; given to cattle as a laxative.
shaped rather like a tether stake this piece of wood was placed in the wall. On this wool could be twisted to form an accumulation of wool. Could also be used for doubling or strengthening threads.
a variant name for ‘crois liaghra’.
a horse’s bit. Seems to be a dialectal variant on the more common word for this – ‘mìreannach’.

contrary to other people hitherto questioned, this informant insists that these were not the spokes in a cartwheel, but rather, the sockets in the actual rim of the wheel into which the spokes slotted.
the cart wheel consisted of four sections put together.
spokes.
a word meaning the same as the previously mentioned ‘connochrochan’; larger than ‘rubhain’.
dolling up.
a thin, scrawny person.
carrying someone, usually a youngster, high on your shoulders with the youngster sitting behind your neck with his legs in front of you.
being told to get lost.
the white background in your eye.
the pupil of your eye.
would be applied to a thin cow or calf. Could also be applied to humans.

item.headword: Tha iad sin ann an deagh thruim
item.description: the opposite of the above [i.e. caoilteach (q.v.)] meaning that the cattle were well fed.
docking of lambs’ tails.
building onto an existing wall.
tempest.
